Ted Charlton, a 58-year-old from rural New Zealand, has been clinically dead and resuscitated seven times due to a rare disorder that prevents his body from regulating temperature and thirst. When his body becomes too hot or cold, it can shut down within minutes—a frightening reality that has led to multiple medical emergencies, including being found floating face-down in a swimming pool and slipping into a coma after a car accident in a river.
Living just outside Dannevirke, Charlton manages his condition through constant vigilance, carefully monitoring what he wears and his surrounding environment. Though the disorder has likely affected him his entire life, it became life-threatening only as he aged. He credits his medic alert bracelet, which he's worn since 1992, with speeding up critical care when he's unable to communicate. On one occasion, a Navy doctor happened to drive past an ambulance scene and intervened; on another, an ambulance officer friend happened to be at the same pool. These fortunate coincidences, combined with the information on his bracelet, have repeatedly saved his life.
Despite the gravity of his situation, Charlton maintains a sense of humor—joking with his father about running out of lives like a cat. His story is a quiet testament to resilience and the importance of taking health seriously, even in small ways. For less than the cost of insuring a car, he notes, a simple medical bracelet can mean the difference between life and death. It's a reminder that preparation and a bit of luck can turn even the most harrowing circumstances into stories of survival worth telling.

item.title: Buffalo who was rancher's 'friend' participates in funeral procession in RS
item.description:
In Nova Hartz, a town in Brazil's Rio Grande do Sul state, a funeral procession took an unusual and deeply moving form. Soberano, a buffalo who had developed a close bond with rancher Marcos Oberdan Bottega, led the cortege honoring his 42-year-old friend. The animal carried Marcos's son, Marquinhos, on his back, while mourners followed behind with the rancher's casket.
The relationship between Marcos and Soberano had become well known in the community, representing more than simply a working relationship between rancher and livestock. The buffalo had become a symbol of the connection between father and son, woven into the fabric of their family life on the ranch. By including Soberano in this final tribute, the family acknowledged the animal as part of their story—a living testament to Marcos's character and the life he built.
During the farewell, an emotional Marquinhos reflected on his father as a hardworking man and made promises that honored both past and future: to care for his mother, to continue looking after Soberano, and to carry forward his father's legacy. "I will be both Marcos and Marquinhos," he said, capturing his commitment to preserving what his father had built. This story reminds us that the bonds we form—whether with people or animals—can transcend the ordinary, and that grief often finds its most authentic expression in the rituals we create to honor those bonds.

item.title: ‘Awed by nature’: fans mourn California’s beloved Jackie the bald eagle, whose legacy soars on
item.description:
Jackie, a bald eagle who made her home at California's Big Bear Lake, has died at age 14, leaving behind millions of devoted followers who watched her daily life unfold through a live-stream camera. For years, viewers around the world tuned in to witness Jackie raising eaglets with her mate Shadow, incubating eggs through snowstorms, and navigating the challenges of wild raptor life. What began as a nature camera became something far more profound—a source of comfort, inspiration, and connection for people facing their own difficulties.
The eagle's impact extended well beyond entertainment. Jackie became an unexpected pioneer in conservation fundraising, helping Friends of Big Bear Valley raise $10 million this year to protect critical habitat around the lake. More than 25,000 donors contributed nearly $5 million toward purchasing a 63-acre ecological corridor, with an additional $5.5 million from OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife. Among Jackie's followers was Gloria Ackman, a retired teacher who, along with her terminally ill husband, found solace watching the eagles' resilience and determination during their darkest months. After her husband's death in December, Ackman continues watching Shadow, finding inspiration in his steadfast presence.
This story matters because it reveals something essential about our relationship with the natural world. Across all boundaries of politics, geography, and belief, people found common ground in their awe of these magnificent birds. Jackie's life—and the community she unknowingly built—reminds us that wildness still speaks to something deep within us, offering meaning, connection, and hope when we need it most.

item.title: Musician from Itu wins doctoral fellowship at 900-year-old university that once had Copernicus as a student
item.description:
A twenty-nine-year-old Brazilian maestro and researcher is embarking on a journey that connects past and present in a quietly poetic way. Leonardo Leite, from the interior city of Itu in São Paulo state, has won a doctoral fellowship to the University of Bologna in Italy—the oldest university in the Western world, founded in 1088 and once home to Copérnico and Umberto Eco. His research focuses on an unperformed 1861 opera called "A Louca" (The Madwoman) by composer Elias Álvares Lobo, also from Itu, whose complete score Leite discovered in Rio de Janeiro archives.
What makes this fellowship especially meaningful is a historical echo: in the nineteenth century, Elias Álvares Lobo himself won a scholarship to study in Italy but was unable to make the trip due to circumstances of the time. More than 160 years later, Leite will carry the composer's work to the very country Lobo never reached. Leite's musical path began at age nine with the caipira viola (a traditional Brazilian string instrument) and has since expanded to classical guitar, accordion, piano, and a French pipe organ in his hometown church. He has studied Italian since he was fourteen and now teaches the language alongside his musical pursuits.
This story is worth a reader's time because it shows how scholarship can be an act of restoration—not just uncovering forgotten art, but completing interrupted journeys across generations. Leite's work brings a piece of Brazilian cultural heritage to an international stage while honoring both his hometown roots and a composer whose dreams were deferred by history.

item.title: 'If you see me, weep': The story behind Europe's 'hunger stones'
item.description:
When Europe's great rivers recede during droughts, they reveal more than sunken ships and wartime relics—they expose stones bearing centuries-old warnings carved into their surfaces. Among the most striking is a message inscribed in German on a boulder in the Elbe River near Děčín, Czech Republic: "If you see me, weep." These are hunger stones, or Hungersteine, markers that spend most years submerged but emerge when water levels drop to dangerous lows. Unlike flood markers that record high water, hunger stones commemorate the opposite: the droughts that brought hardship to communities dependent on rivers for transport, trade, and survival.
For centuries, residents along rivers like the Elbe, Danube, and Rhine have carved dates and inscriptions onto these stones during severe droughts—some bearing years as far back as 1616. Historical research has shown these weren't merely symbolic memorials. A 2020 study found that many inscriptions on Elbe hunger stones correspond closely with documented periods of exceptionally low water levels, suggesting they served as practical records of river depth. When waters dropped, barges carrying grain and timber couldn't navigate shallow channels, disrupting vital trade routes. Crop failures followed, along with rising prices and famine. The famous "weep" inscription from 1904 represents just one chapter in a much longer chronicle of drought.
These stones have captured renewed attention during recent European droughts in 2020 and 2022, with media describing them as ominous harbingers. Yet they're perhaps better understood as a bridge between past and present—a reminder that communities have long grappled with water scarcity, and found ways to document their struggles for future generations. In an era of climate uncertainty, these submerged chronicles offer both historical perspective and quiet testament to human resilience.

item.title: At 96, grandmother travels over 400 km to go to the cinema for the first time and watch her grandson with Down syndrome in a film
item.description:
At 96 years old, Olinda Cecília Deliberali experienced something most people remember from childhood: her first trip to the cinema. The grandmother traveled over 400 kilometers from her home in Planalto, in northern Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, to Porto Alegre for a premiere screening of a film starring her grandson, Gabriel Deliberali. Gabriel, an actor with Down syndrome, is one of the protagonists in "Colegas e o Herdeiro," a film whose cast includes several performers with Down syndrome. The movie follows a group of friends on an adventurous journey to Uruguay that unexpectedly entangles them with gem smugglers.
The bond between Olinda and Gabriel runs deep. According to Gabriel's mother, Janeci, her son's first smile at two months old happened in his grandmother's arms. A devotee of Santa Rita, Olinda has prayed 22 Ave Marias for Gabriel every day since his birth. During the premiere, Gabriel called his grandmother his "shining pearl" and expressed his joy at sharing this milestone with her. Gabriel emphasizes that the film carries an important message about inclusion, often reminding audiences to "look at the child, not at the Down syndrome" — to see the person first, before any disability.
This story captures something quietly powerful: a grandmother's unwavering belief in her grandson's potential, a young actor's achievement in a medium working toward greater representation, and the simple beauty of shared firsts. It reminds us that meaningful experiences aren't bound by age, and that love and support can help open doors we never imagined walking through.
